citation.title: AI Ethics: An Empirical Study on the Views of Practitioners and Lawmakers

reading.source_scope_note: Human survey of ethical-principle/challenge endorsements, not a direct model audit, psychological-bias experiment or observed organizational compliance study. Reporting/inference issues prevent treating rank comparisons as reliable evidence for a novel behavioural mechanism.
access_limits: All14 extracted pages read, including survey design, demographic figure/caption, principle/challenge rankings, correlation and t-test tables, perceived-impact ratings, validity discussion and references.

External Zenodo replication package, individual survey responses, respondent-role recoding, questionnaires and later publication versions were not independently retrieved or rerun. No quantitative result is inferred from a plot alone.

study.design: Convenience/network recruitment; English and Chinese survey; endorsement frequencies, dense ranks, rank correlations and aggregate-rank t-tests

summary: The study reports broad endorsement of known principles and perceived implementation challenges. It supplies no well-defined new behaviour, and its group-rank tests, denominator reporting and severity/time interpretation have major limitations. The repo receives the full review and queue update; no ontology ID or selected-paper slot is added merely to represent this file.

findings.term: Survey respondents raise existing implicit-bias concerns
findings.definition: Participants identify implicit and cognitive bias as possible ethical challenges, without the survey itself measuring a model's bias or a distinct new mechanism.
findings.novelty_rationale: The ontology already contains implicit bias. A quoted concern is not a new behaviour, direct empirical replication or independent paper establishing model-level effects.

evidence.quote: Implicit biases in AI algorithms such as data

findings.evidence_scope: Open-ended respondent suggestions are summarized; no example model outputs, experimental contrasts, effect-size estimates, bias subtypes or model training manipulation are supplied.
findings.boundary: Endorsement or concern is not observed prevalence or verified causal harm. The paper is reviewed but is not added as a model-bias evidence source merely because respondents mention the term.

methodological_limits: The supplied version is a2022 preprint under review, despite a2023 filename. No claim is made about the status or corrections of a later version.

Recruitment uses industrial contacts, social media, personal links and law forums. Calling the99 respondents representative does not establish probability sampling or representation of all practitioners/lawmakers.

TablesI/V label29 lawmakers and52 practitioners (81 total),18 fewer than the stated99 complete respondents. The role-to-comparison-group mapping and omitted respondents are not clearly explained in the text.

Figure3 and group tables do not always reconcile under an assumed common denominator: for example pooled sustainability endorsement61.6% of99 implies about61 respondents, whereas TableI lists24+45=69 across the two stated groups. Raw data and coding are needed to resolve subset, definition or transcription differences.

A single law-practitioner category is used as the lawmaker group label. It does not establish every member is a legislator or public policymaker; other roles and expertise classifications also require care.

Twenty countries and five continents do not imply balanced cultural coverage; the supplied demographic summary is heavily Asia-weighted (77/99). Exact country-wide or culture-wide effects are not identified.

Spearman correlation tests whether two item rankings covary, not whether groups differ on a particular item. An overall significant rho=.819 does not make the fairness rank5 versus7 difference statistically significant.

Spearman assesses monotonic association, not necessarily linear dependence as described in the text. Positive correlation does not establish equality, agreement in absolute endorsements or common awareness.

The t-tests use21 principle ranks or15 challenge ranks as observations, not99 individual respondents. Corresponding items are matched across groups; an independent-samples test ignores that pairing and participant-level uncertainty.

Dense ranks include many ties, so mean-rank differences depend on ranking/tie structure. Comparing such averages is not a valid substitute for testing respondent-level priority distributions; rank-level N is not participant N.

TableIII is internally inconsistent: mean difference−.23810 divided by SE .53875 is approximately−.442, consistent with two-sided p around.661, not the printed t=.942. The reported t and p cannot both describe that ordinary40-df test.
TableIII also reports Levene F=.117 with p=.051; the combination requires verification, and the prose's description of p>.05 as slightly significant is incorrect under its stated threshold.
For challenges the prose repeats Levene p=.051, but TableVII gives F=.519,p=.477. Do not silently substitute one value or treat the table/prose as verified consistent.

Nonsignificant t-tests (reported p=.661/.207) do not show that groups equally consider the principles/challenges, have equivalent awareness or share identical perceptions. No equivalence margin/test is supplied.

Individual differences in ranks are descriptive; no reliable item-level test or multiple-comparison procedure supports broad claims of statistically significant differences for particular principles/challenges.

Perceived-impact ratings classify insignificant/minor/moderate as short-term and major/catastrophic as long-term. This conflates severity with duration; the cross-sectional survey does not measure longitudinal effects.

Endorsing lack of ethical knowledge as a challenge (reported81.8%) does not mean81.8% personally lack knowledge, nor demonstrate that training quickly repairs that barrier. Proposed training effects are untested.
Agreement that no legal framework or monitoring body is a challenge is a perception at the2021–2022 survey period, not a verified current inventory of laws/regulators.
Only a preselected subset of seven challenges against six principles is rated for severity. It does not establish all ethics barriers' objective impacts, causal effects or all-system priorities.

Interpretation differences, technical constraints and conflicting duties can be legitimate governance issues rather than cognitive failures. Machine distortion is listed without a sufficiently precise operational definition for a new behaviour entry.
Author consensus and feedback are described as safeguards but do not independently establish instrument reliability, construct validity, reproducibility or absence of shared analytic mistakes.
Some bibliography metadata is visibly inconsistent: reference3 has a DevOps-forecast title attached to a Reuters recruitment-bias URL; repeated Lu and Leikas works are not independent corroborations.
All primary cited studies and replication materials remain unread here; no tested behavioural source or quantitative ontology relationship is inferred from their bibliography entries.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Jakesch's group-value differences are also bounded by recruitment and missingness. Khan additionally tests item ranks rather than respondent-level preferences; its significance claims cannot be compared directly with adjusted participant-level regressions.

Carroll's relative utility coefficients and Khan's endorsement ranks are different estimands. A list of top principles in each paper is not an objective ethical ranking or evidence that lower-ranked values may be ignored.

The distinction between correlation and agreement applies here too: positive rank association does not establish equality, and its significance does not test whether particular group judgments differ.

deferred.reason: Named as a challenge but not defined/operationalized precisely enough in the supplied paper. Do not invent a mechanism from the label.
A broad governance trade-off category, not necessarily a distinct behaviour; perceived severity is not an observed causal effect.
Respondents endorse a perceived barrier; individual lack of knowledge or a new metacognitive behaviour is not objectively measured.
A documented inference issue in this paper, not a newly studied cognitive disposition. Preserve the methodological lesson without a new ID.

limitations: No ontology changes or paper-count inflation for this file; only the reviewed record and corpus manifest are updated.
Unreliable denominators, tests and causal/time claims remain explicit; the supplied version rather than filename date determines citation.
